title: Regulated Crypto Trading: Institutional Execution and Settlement
summary: BitGo supports institutional market structure through regulated custody, trading access, integrated settlement infrastructure, and tools for managing capital across external trading venues.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


-


Institutional crypto trading is moving toward a model where responsibility for custody, execution, and settlement is distributed across distinct parties rather than concentrated within a single trading venue.


-


Separating custody from trading gives institutions more flexibility in how they access liquidity, including through exchanges, prime services, and OTC markets, without requiring the trading provider to also serve as the custodian.


-


Keeping assets within a custody-centered framework can improve both capital efficiency and risk management.


-


BitGo supports this market structure through regulated custody, trading access, integrated settlement infrastructure, and tools for managing capital across external trading venues.


Crypto's first decade was built around a simple trading model. The same exchange often held customer assets, matched trades, and managed settlement. For market participants focused on access and speed, that structure worked. It also concentrated a significant amount of trust in a single venue.


The collapse of[FTX](https://www.investopedia.com/what-went-wrong-with-ftx-6828447) exposed the weaknesses of that model. Institutions were reminded that the venue executing a trade and the entity safeguarding assets do not necessarily serve the same function. That lesson, unfortunately, was not limited to a single firm's failure, and raised broader questions about custody, counterparty exposure, and what controls should exist between trade execution and final settlement.


That period changed how institutions evaluate crypto trading infrastructure. Execution quality still matters, but it is no longer the only consideration. Institutions now examine where assets are held, how settlement occurs, what happens if a counterparty fails, and whether trading activity can take place without exposing assets to unnecessary venue risk.


As a result, the conversation around institutional crypto trading has expanded beyond liquidity alone. The question is no longer whether liquidity exists. Exchanges, market makers, and OTC venues provide ample access to markets. The challenge is accessing that liquidity while maintaining control of assets, managing settlement risk, and operating within a framework that can satisfy investors, auditors, and regulators.


That challenge is shaping the next phase of institutional crypto market structure. Custody, execution, and settlement are increasingly being treated as separate functions rather than responsibilities concentrated within a single platform.


## Separating Custody From Trading with Off-Exchange Settlement and Prime Brokerage


An institution trading across multiple exchanges often faces a practical problem. Liquidity may be available on several venues, but accessing that liquidity traditionally required assets to be sitting on each venue before trading could begin.


As a result, firms frequently maintained balances across multiple exchanges so capital was already in place when an opportunity appeared. The more venues a firm wanted to access, the more assets needed to be distributed across those venues. Trading activity and asset location became closely connected because assets had to move to liquidity before a trade could occur.


Off-exchange settlement changes that model by separating execution from custody. Rather than depositing assets on exchange before trading, institutions can keep assets with a custodian while accessing liquidity on the exchange. This reduces the amount of capital held directly on exchanges simply to maintain market access.


Further separation of custody and trading also comes through prime brokerage models where institutions can access liquidity across multiple venues and counterparties through a centralized trading relationship. Rather than onboarding and maintaining separate balances across multiple venues and relationships, institutions can access liquidity while assets remain in custody, and settlement occurs afterward according to an agreed process between the parties. Because assets are not sitting on each trading venue before execution, institutions can reduce the amount of capital exposed to any single exchange.


The execution models are different, i.e., with off-exchange settlement institutions access a particular exchange while through a prime institution instead trade with one counterparty that provides access to liquidity sourced from multiple venues and counterparties. What connects the two models is accessing liquidity does not require assets to be held wherever the liquidity resides. This matters as institutional crypto markets continue to mature and gives institutions more flexibility in how they organize trading activity.


A firm can access liquidity from multiple venues without approaching each venue as a separate custody destination. Assets remain within a consistent custody framework that fit their governance and risk requirements while trading activity occurs across exchanges, dealers, and liquidity providers. As custody and execution become separate functions, institutions are paying closer attention to what happens after execution occurs.


## Why Settlement Has Become a Risk Management Issue


Keeping assets in custody solves one challenge, but every trade still needs to settle. Once a transaction is executed, the buyer owes payment and the seller owes assets, and neither party wants to deliver first and take the risk that the other side fails to perform.[Delivery-versus-payment](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/dvp.asp) settlement addresses that exposure by linking the two transfers so assets and payment are exchanged together. When settlement can also occur within a qualified custody framework, institutions can complete the trade without moving assets outside that environment simply to satisfy the settlement obligation.


Managing settlement for a single transaction is relatively straightforward. The challenge grows as trading activity expands. A firm may have trades settling with multiple exchanges, dealers, and liquidity providers throughout the day. Each transaction creates another obligation that needs to be completed before the trade can truly be considered finished.


Those obligations do not always settle at the same time or through the same process. One counterparty may settle immediately while another settles later in the day. Payment instructions may need to be reconciled across multiple systems, and assets expected from one transaction may be needed to support another. As trading activity increases, institutions need a reliable process for tracking obligations and resolving discrepancies before they affect liquidity or trading operations.


As those obligations accumulate, visibility becomes more important. Firms need to know which transactions have settled, which remain outstanding, and whether expected assets or payments have arrived. A delay, reconciliation issue, or settlement failure can create uncertainty that extends beyond the original trade, especially when capital from one transaction is expected to support another. If funds expected from a completed trade do not arrive on time, a firm may need to delay additional transactions, source liquidity elsewhere, or adjust positions while the issue is resolved.


This is why institutions pay close attention to what happens after execution. Accessing liquidity is only part of the trading process. Firms also need confidence that transactions will settle as expected, counterparties will fulfill their obligations, and trading activity can continue without disruption when volumes increase.


As responsibility for custody, execution, and settlement becomes less concentrated within a single entity, the infrastructure connecting those activities becomes more important. Institutions need transactions to move from execution through settlement in a way that remains visible and reliable as trading activity grows.


## Managing Liquidity Across a Fragmented Market


A firm that wants access to liquidity across multiple exchanges often keeps assets on multiple exchanges. That approach keeps capital close to the market, but it also spreads assets across a growing number of venues and accounts.


As those balances become more fragmented, managing them becomes an operational challenge. Trading and treasury teams need visibility into how much capital is available across venues, where it is sitting, and where it needs to move next. Without a consolidated view, teams may need to check balances venue by venue and manually transfer assets to rebalance positions, meet margin requirements, or take advantage of trading opportunities. A firm can have sufficient capital overall and still be unable to deploy it efficiently because that capital is sitting in the wrong place.


The right operational infrastructure can make that capital easier to manage. A unified view across custody and exchange accounts gives teams a clearer picture of available buying power, while tools for moving assets between those accounts can reduce the manual work required to reposition capital. Firms can then manage liquidity across venues without treating every exchange balance as a separate operational workflow.


That same visibility can help firms understand what capital is available and what has already been committed across trading and settlement obligations. Instead of relying on a collection of disconnected venue balances, teams can manage capital across custody, exchanges, and other trading relationships through a more coordinated operating model.


Capital efficiency becomes part of risk management because institutions no longer have to choose between maintaining control of assets and accessing liquidity. The same custody framework that improves visibility and control can also make capital easier to deploy across trading, settlement, and financing activities.


## Regulation Is Reinforcing the Shift


Institutions began separating custody, execution, and settlement because they wanted greater control over how assets were held, moved, and settled. Regulators are moving in the same direction.


The Digital Asset Market[CLARITY Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/3633) passed the House and remains one of the most important proposals shaping U.S. digital asset market structure. The framework would require stronger customer asset segregation, establish standards for qualified digital asset custodians, and create clearer oversight for digital commodity spot markets.


Those expectations align closely with the infrastructure many institutions are already building. Assets are held with qualified custodians. Trading activity, settlement activity, and asset movements are recorded in a way that can be reviewed internally and shared with auditors, regulators, and investors when needed. That visibility becomes particularly important when activity spans multiple venues, counterparties, and settlement workflows that must ultimately be reconciled into a single record of ownership and activity.


Institutions also need a consistent record of activity across both onchain transactions and offchain trading systems. As trading activity expands, firms need to understand where assets were held, how they moved, and how settlement obligations were managed throughout the process.


The market structure emerging around institutional crypto trading reflects those requirements. Clear asset segregation, auditable records, and reporting that connects custody, trading activity, and settlement are becoming part of the foundation for operating in a regulated market.

## FAQs


### What is off-exchange settlement?


Off-exchange settlement allows institutions to trade with exchanges and liquidity providers while assets remain with a custodian. Instead of depositing assets onto every trading venue in advance, firms can execute trades and settle the resulting obligations afterward through defined settlement processes.


### Why do institutions separate custody from execution?


Separating custody from execution allows institutions to access liquidity without relying on a trading venue to hold assets. The model can reduce exchange exposure while giving firms greater control over how assets are stored, moved, and monitored.


### What is counterparty risk in crypto trading?


Counterparty risk is the possibility that another party fails to fulfill its obligations after a trade is executed. The risk exists between execution and final settlement, when assets and payments still need to be exchanged between counterparties.


### What is qualified custody in crypto?


Qualified custody refers to holding digital assets with a regulated custodian that is authorized to safeguard client assets. Many institutions use qualified custodians to support asset segregation, security requirements, compliance obligations, and operational controls.


### What is crypto prime brokerage?


Crypto[prime brokerage](https://www.bitgo.com/products/prime/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=prime&utm_campaign=regulated_crypto_trading) brings together services such as custody, trading access, financing, lending, settlement, and reporting within a single operating framework. The goal is to help institutions manage trading activity more efficiently across multiple venues and counterparties.


### Why is regulated custody important?


Regulated custody provides a foundation for asset segregation, reporting, and operational controls. As institutional participation grows and regulatory expectations evolve, many firms view regulated custody as a core part of managing trading, settlement, and risk.
